ap_macroeconomics-m01.stem: A government that ran a budget deficit last year runs a budget surplus this year and uses the whole surplus to repay borrowing. Which statement correctly describes what happens to the national debt this year?

options.text: The national debt falls to zero, because a surplus cancels all earlier deficits.
options.why: A single year's surplus reduces, but rarely eliminates, the accumulated debt.

options.text: The national debt increases, because a surplus means the government is still borrowing.
options.why: A surplus means the government is spending less than it collects, so it is not adding to its borrowing.

options.text: The national debt is unchanged, because a surplus only affects the budget deficit.
options.why: Using the surplus to repay borrowing reduces the accumulated debt.

options.text: The national debt increases, because repaying debt raises interest payments.
options.why: Repaying borrowing lowers the debt on which interest is paid.

options.text: The national debt decreases, because the surplus is used to repay part of the money previously borrowed.
options.why: A surplus used for repayment reduces the stock of outstanding government borrowing, which is the national debt.

options.why: Money growth does not raise long-run productivity.

options.text: An increase in human capital, because workers are producing more.

options.why: The number of workers has not changed, only the capital each worker uses.

options.text: A fall in the natural rate of unemployment, because machines replace workers.
options.why: A change in the natural rate is not the source of this productivity gain.

options.text: An increase in physical capital per worker, which raises labor productivity.
options.why: Machinery is physical capital, and more capital per worker raises output per worker.

options.text: The interest rate falls permanently, because the money supply is larger.
options.why: Rapid money growth raises inflation and the nominal interest rate over time.

options.text: Real output rises rapidly, because the larger money supply raises long-run productivity.
options.why: Money growth does not raise long-run real output.

options.text: The price level is stable, because new money offsets the slow growth of output.
options.why: Money growth that exceeds output growth raises prices.

options.text: Unemployment falls to zero, because spending rises with the money supply.
options.why: Rapid money growth does not eliminate unemployment.

options.text: The price level rises rapidly, because the money supply grows much faster than real output.
options.why: Money growth far above output growth means more money chases the same goods, which pushes prices up continuously.

ap_macroeconomics-m06.stem: A central bank wants to lower the inflation rate in the short run by reducing aggregate demand. Which statement best describes the cost shown by the short-run Phillips curve?

options.text: The short-run Phillips curve shifts up, because lower demand raises costs.
options.why: The policy moves the economy along the curve, not up with a shift.

options.text: Unemployment falls below its starting level, because lower inflation reduces uncertainty.
options.why: On the short-run curve, lower inflation is associated with higher unemployment.

options.text: Unemployment is unchanged, because the short-run curve is vertical.
options.why: The vertical curve is the long-run curve, not the short-run curve.

options.text: Inflation rises, because lower demand raises expectations of inflation.
options.why: Lower demand lowers inflation along the short-run curve.

options.text: Unemployment rises above its starting level, because lower inflation requires moving down along the curve.
options.why: Along a downward-sloping short-run curve, lower inflation comes with higher unemployment.

ap_macroeconomics-m06.stem: A temporary rise in oil prices raises firms' costs, shifting the short-run Phillips curve up. Which statement best describes the effect on the trade-off facing policymakers?

options.text: The long-run Phillips curve shifts right, because oil prices change the natural rate.
options.why: A temporary supply shock moves the short-run curve, not the long-run curve.

options.text: Every unemployment rate now comes with higher inflation, so reducing inflation costs more unemployment.
options.why: An upward-shifted short-run curve puts higher inflation at each unemployment rate, so the trade-off worsens.

options.text: Every unemployment rate now comes with lower inflation, so the trade-off improves.
options.why: An upward shift raises, not lowers, inflation at each unemployment rate.

options.text: Unemployment falls at every inflation rate, because costs are higher.
options.why: A rise in costs does not lower unemployment at each inflation rate.

options.text: The trade-off disappears, because oil prices are outside policymakers' control.
options.why: The short-run trade-off still exists on the new, higher curve.
